props.title: The Crowd
props.initialSlug: Innovative tracking shots through office spaces

sections.content: The Crowd stands as King Vidor's masterpiece of American social realism, revolutionizing how cinema portrayed ordinary life. The film follows John Sims, an average office worker lost in Manhattan's sea of humanity, crafting an intimate portrait of urban alienation that influenced generations of filmmakers. Its innovative cinematography, particularly the sweeping shots of endless office desks and towering skyscrapers, directly inspired later works like The Apartment (1960) and Brazil (1985). Vidor's unflinching look at a common man's struggles broke from Hollywood's typical glamorization, establishing a template for neo-realist storytelling.

sections.content: The film's influence extends deeply into post-war Italian Neorealism, with directors like De Sica and Rossellini adopting its street-level perspective and focus on working-class struggles. Bicycle Thieves (1948) particularly echoes The Crowd's father-son dynamics and urban desperation. Modern filmmakers continue drawing from Vidor's techniques - Manchester by the Sea (2016) and Marriage Story (2019) share its intimate approach to personal crisis and family dynamics.

Vidor's groundbreaking visual style transformed how cities were depicted on screen. His vertiginous shots looking down office building atria and bustling street scenes created a grammar of urban alienation that influenced Metropolis (1927) and later noir classics like The Third Man (1949). The film's innovative mobile camera work, tracking through crowds and following characters in fluid motion, predated the French New Wave's street photography by decades. sections.content: The Crowd's lasting impact on American cinema can't be overstated. Its DNA runs through the social problem films of the 1930s like Our Daily Bread (1934) and into the post-war realism of On the Waterfront (1954). Modern directors like Kenneth Lonergan and Kelly Reichardt continue its tradition of unvarnished American life. The film's exploration of mental health and career disappointment feels startlingly contemporary, presaging works like Revolutionary Road (2008) and Falling Down (1993).
